title: Muting, Joining, and the Digits
summary: The last of the writing system: the mark that takes a consonant's vowel away, the subjoined forms by which two consonants are written together, the doubled consonants that fill everyday Telugu words, and the ten digits.

script.heading: The digits — తెలుగు అంకెలు
notes: The digits are decimal and positional, exactly like the European ones, which are themselves of Indian descent. ౨౦౨౬ (2026) (2026) is 2026.

Modern Telugu writes numbers with the European digits almost everywhere. The Telugu digits are met in older books, on some official documents, and in ornamental use — a reader should know them and a writer need not use them.

rules.heading: The Pollu — ్
rules.statement: A consonant carries the vowel అ (¶8), and a vowel sign may replace it (¶20). To give a consonant **no vowel at all**, a mark called the **పొల్లు** (pollu) is written under it. It is the same device other Indian scripts call the *virāma* or *halant*. A consonant with a pollu is a bare consonant, and this is the only way to write one.

examples.gloss: k — with the pollu, no vowel

footnotes: In running text the pollu is written chiefly at the end of a word or in a foreign name. Within a word, two consonants coming together are joined instead, as the next rule shows.

rules.heading: Joining Two Consonants — ఒత్తు
rules.statement: Where two consonants meet inside a word with no vowel between them, Telugu does not write a pollu on the first. Instead the **second** consonant is written in a reduced form **beneath** the first. That subjoined form is called an **ఒత్తు** (ottu), and the two together make a **conjunct** — one written unit standing for two consonants and one vowel.

paradigms.caption: Conjuncts
paradigms.footnote: The last is written with the anusvāra rather than an ottu, because the first consonant is a nasal of the second's own varga (¶18).

rules.heading: The Ottu Loses its Headstroke
rules.statement: A consonant written as an **ottu** is reduced: it is smaller, it sits below the line of the letter above it, and it **loses its తలకట్టు** (¶6). This is what makes conjuncts hard to read at first — the subjoined letter no longer looks like the letter on the chart. Learning to recognise the thirty-six ottu shapes is a second labour after learning the thirty-six letters, and there is no way round it.

examples.gloss: the full letter against its subjoined form
kka — the same letter twice, once full and once reduced

rules.heading: Doubled Consonants
rules.statement: Telugu is full of **doubled** consonants, and the doubling is heard as well as written: the consonant is held longer, as the *t* is held in English "hot topic" but not in "hotel". A doubled consonant is written as a conjunct of a letter with itself. Doubling distinguishes words and is not an ornament of spelling.

rules.heading: The Digits
rules.statement: Telugu has its own ten digits, **౦ (0) (0) ౧ (1) (1) ౨ (2) (2) ౩ (3) (3) ౪ (4) (4) ౫ (5) (5) ౬ (6) (6) ౭ (7) (7) ౮ (8) (8) ౯ (9) (9)**. They are decimal and positional, as the European digits are — the European digits being themselves Indian by descent. Modern Telugu writes numbers with the European figures almost everywhere; the Telugu ones survive in older printing and in ornament, and a reader should know them without needing to use them.

examples.note: sunna — the Telugu word for zero, and for the anusvāra's little circle too

rules.heading: Reading a Whole Word
rules.statement: Everything needed to read Telugu is now in hand. Take each written unit in turn; find its main consonant; look above, below and to the right for a vowel sign; look below for an **ottu**, which adds a consonant before the vowel; and sound the result. A word has as many syllables as it has such units — a conjunct being one unit, not two.

examples.note: pu-sta-kaṃ — three units, three syllables, though four consonants
te-lu-gu — three units, each with its own sign

options: It lengthens the vowel.
It takes away the consonant's inherent vowel, leaving a bare consonant.
It nasalises the vowel.
It doubles the consonant.
drills.explanation: క is *ka*; క్ is *k*. It is the only way to write a consonant with no vowel, and other Indian scripts call the same device the virāma.
౫ (5) (5) is five, *aidu*. The digits run ౦ (0) (0) ౧ (1) (1) ౨ (2) (2) ౩ (3) (3) ౪ (4) (4) ౫ (5) (5) ౬ (6) (6) ౭ (7) (7) ౮ (8) (8) ౯ (9) (9) and are positional like the European ones.
౩ (3) (3) is three, *mūḍu*.

options: A vowel sign written above a consonant.
A consonant written in reduced form beneath another.
A mark of punctuation.
The name of the Telugu digit zero.
drills.explanation: It is the subjoined form by which a second consonant is written under the first, making a conjunct. The digit zero is *sunnā*.

drills.stem: Inside a word, two consonants meet with no vowel between them. How does Telugu write them?
options: With a pollu on the first consonant.
With the second consonant subjoined beneath the first.
With a vowel sign between them.
With the anusvāra.
drills.explanation: The pollu is used chiefly at the end of a word and in foreign names; within a word the two are joined into one written unit. The anusvāra does the work only where the first consonant is a nasal of the second's varga.

options: ka
kka
kaka
k
drills.explanation: One unit, two consonants, one vowel: *kka*, a doubled k. The same letter is written twice — once full, once as an ottu beneath it.

drills.stem: Why is a subjoined consonant hard to recognise at first?
options: It is written in a different alphabet.
It is reduced in size and loses its తలకట్టు, so it no longer matches the chart.
It is written above the letter, where the eye does not look.
It stands for a different sound from the full letter.
drills.explanation: The sound is the same; only the shape is reduced. Learning the thirty-six ottu forms is a second labour after learning the thirty-six letters, and it cannot be avoided.

drills.stem: How is the doubled consonant of **అమ్మ** sounded?
options: As a single m, the doubling being a spelling convention.
As an m held longer, as in English 'hot topic' rather than 'hotel'.
As two separate syllables, am-ma-a.
As an aspirated m.
drills.explanation: Doubling is heard, not merely written, and it distinguishes words. English doubles consonants across a word boundary and almost never within one, which is why the habit must be learned.

drills.stem: Which of these words contain a **doubled** consonant?
options: అమ్మ
ఇల్లు
నది
పిల్ల
drills.explanation: అమ్మ has mm, ఇల్లు has ll, పిల్ల has ll. నది is *nadi*, two plain consonants with a vowel between them and nothing doubled.
The digits are positional exactly as the European ones are: ౨ (2) (2) then ౦ (0) (0) is twenty.

drills.stem: In **పండు** the nasal is written with ం rather than with an ottu. Why?
options: Because ణ has no subjoined form.
Because the nasal belongs to the same varga as the డ that follows, and the anusvāra writes just such a nasal.
Because the word is a loanword.
Because ం is easier to write.
drills.explanation: The anusvāra takes the nasal of the following consonant's varga (¶18). డ is retroflex, so ం is sounded ṇ — and no ottu is needed.

drills.stem: Which statements about the pollu and the ottu are correct?
options: Both have the effect of removing a vowel between two consonants.
The ottu is used chiefly inside a word, the pollu chiefly at its end.
A consonant written as an ottu keeps its full shape.
The pollu is the same device other Indian scripts call the virāma.
drills.explanation: The ottu is reduced and loses its headstroke — that is precisely what makes conjuncts hard to read. The two devices solve the same problem in two positions.
Three: *pu-sta-kaṃ*. The conjunct స్త is one written unit and one syllable, though it holds two consonants. Answering four counts consonants instead of units.

Five: p, s, t, k and the m of the final anusvāra. The conjunct holds two of them and the anusvāra is a consonant sound though it is written as a mark. Compare the three syllables of the previous question — the two counts are different questions about the same word.
Two: *i-llu*. The independent vowel ఇ makes the first, and the conjunct ల్లు the second. Three would be the answer if the doubled l were counted as two units.

drills.stem: A learner meets a written unit with a mark above it and a reduced shape below it. What are they looking at?
options: Two separate letters written too close together.
A consonant with a vowel sign above and an ottu below — one syllable of two consonants.
A consonant with two vowel signs.
A digit.
drills.explanation: Above is where vowel signs go and below is where consonants are subjoined (¶22, ¶27). The unit is one syllable: the ottu supplies a consonant *before* the vowel that the sign names.
One hundred and one. The middle digit is ౦ (0) (0), *sunnā* — the same word Telugu uses for the anusvāra's little circle.

drills.stem: Why does modern Telugu print rarely use ౦ (0) (0) ౧ (1) (1) ౨ (2) (2) ౩ (3) (3)?
options: Because the digits were abolished.
Because the European digits have displaced them in ordinary use, though the Telugu ones remain in older books and in ornament.
Because Telugu has no numbers of its own.
Because they are not positional and so are inconvenient.
drills.explanation: They are positional and perfectly serviceable — the European digits are Indian by descent. Their retreat is a matter of practice, not of merit, and a reader still needs to know them.

options: It has three written units and three syllables.
Every one of its consonants carries a vowel sign.
It contains a conjunct.
It begins with a consonant, not a vowel.
drills.explanation: *te-lu-gu* — three units, each a consonant with its own sign, and no consonant subjoined to any other. It opens with త, which is why no independent vowel letter is written (¶7).
Three: n, and then ḷ twice, the doubling being written as a conjunct and heard as a held consonant. Answering two counts the doubled ళ once, which is exactly what the doubling exists to prevent.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985.
